## What Is an Employer of Record in Puerto Rico


In Puerto Rico, this arrangement carries particular weight. The island operates under a dual legal framework: it follows federal U.S. law, including federal payroll taxes like FICA and FUTA, while also maintaining its own labor code with requirements that differ from any U.S. state. Mandatory benefits, termination rules, and local tax obligations all require careful attention.


An EOR steps in as the entity of record with Puerto Rico's Department of Labor and the Hacienda, the island's treasury department, so you can[hire globally without the complexity](https://www.bolto.com/employer-of-record) of setting up a local legal entity.


### How This Differs from Hiring Directly


When you hire directly in Puerto Rico, your company must register as a local employer, open a local payroll account, and stay current with both federal and Commonwealth-level requirements. An EOR absorbs that administrative and legal burden. Your team member works for you in practice; the EOR holds the employment relationship on paper and keeps it compliant.


This is worth understanding before reviewing the specific rules that govern Puerto Rico employment, because those rules are what make the[EOR international hiring model](https://www.bolto.com/blog/eor-international-global-hiring-expansion-guide) practical for most companies hiring there without a local entity already in place.


## Employment Laws and Compliance Requirements in Puerto Rico


Puerto Rico operates under a hybrid legal framework that blends U.S. federal employment law with its own local labor code, and the combination creates more employer obligations than most U.S. states impose.


Here's a quick look at the key requirements you'll need to account for.


### Federal Laws That Apply in Puerto Rico


Because Puerto Rico is a U.S. territory, federal employment laws apply there just as they do on the mainland:


- The Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) sets federal minimum wage floors, overtime rules, and child labor standards. Puerto Rico's own minimum wage can exceed the federal floor depending on the sector.
- The Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) requires eligible employers to offer up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave annually for qualifying family or medical reasons.
- Title VII, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), and the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) all apply, prohibiting discrimination based on race, disability, age, and other protected characteristics.
- Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA) payroll taxes, Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA), and federal income tax withholding requirements apply just as they do for mainland U.S. employees.


### Puerto Rico-Specific Labor Protections


Local law adds a second layer that often goes beyond what federal law requires:


- Puerto Rico's Working Hours and Days Act generally limits the standard workweek, and overtime rules can differ from straight FLSA calculations.
- [Puerto Rico Law 80 unjust dismissal](https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=b642185b-0542-4444-b9fa-52d360e565dc) governs unjust dismissal. Without just cause, employers generally owe severance known as "meseta," which scales with tenure.
- Employees are typically entitled to paid vacation leave that accrues on a tiered monthly schedule under Puerto Rico's Minimum Wage, Vacation and Sick Leave Act: 6 days per year during year one, 9 days per year from years one through five, 12 days per year from years five through fifteen, and 15 days per year after fifteen years of service. Sick leave accrues at 1 day per month, up to 12 days per year. (29 L.P.R.A. § 250d, 2025 Laws of Puerto Rico)
- A Christmas bonus is generally required under Law 148 for eligible employees, tied to hours worked during the qualifying period.
- Puerto Rico maintains its own income tax system separate from the U.S. federal system, so payroll withholding and filings run through the Puerto Rico Department of the Treasury (Hacienda), not solely through the IRS. The[IRS guidance on Puerto Rico income](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc901) outlines how bona fide residents interact with both tax systems.


Getting this right matters. Missteps on severance, leave, or tax filings can create real exposure, and the dual-layer framework is easy to underestimate if you're used to hiring only on the U.S. mainland. Reviewing the[best EOR companies for global hiring](https://www.bolto.com/blog/best-eor-companies-global-hiring-guide) can help you identify which provider handles both layers effectively.


*This is general information, not legal advice. Rules vary by situation and change over time, so consult a qualified employment lawyer for your specific circumstances.*

## Cost of Hiring in Puerto Rico with an EOR vs. a Local Entity


Puerto Rico sits in an interesting middle ground: it is a U.S. territory, so you avoid international wire transfers and currency conversion, but it has its own tax code, labor laws, and statutory benefits that differ from the 50 states. That gap is where costs can surprise you.


### Setting Up a Local Entity vs. Using an EOR


If you go the local entity route, you are looking at registering with the Puerto Rico Department of State, obtaining a merchant registration certificate, registering for Employer Identification Numbers at both the federal and territorial level, and setting up payroll accounts with the Puerto Rico Department of the Treasury. Before hiring your first person, legal and administrative setup costs can run several thousand dollars or more, depending on legal fees and structure chosen, and the timeline typically stretches weeks or months.


An EOR absorbs that setup entirely. You pay a service fee per employee, and the EOR already holds the registrations, handles tax filings, and administers statutory benefits on your behalf.


### What Drives the Cost Difference


- Puerto Rico requires employers to contribute to a local unemployment system (SUTA, or State Unemployment Tax Act) separately from federal FUTA obligations, which adds a layer many mainland-only payroll setups are not configured for.
- Statutory benefits like the Christmas bonus and mandatory vacation and sick leave accruals carry real dollar costs that an EOR prices into its model, so there are no unexpected year-end surprises.
- Compliance errors in Puerto Rico can trigger audits at both the territorial and federal level, and the cost of remediation typically exceeds the EOR service fee many times over. For a broader look at cross-border hiring, see our guide on[how to hire international workers](https://www.bolto.com/blog/hire-international-workers-guide-us-employers) as a US employer.


For most early-stage or single-market teams, the EOR route is the lower-cost path until headcount makes the fixed overhead of a local entity worthwhile.

## EOR vs. Local Entity in Puerto Rico: Which Is Right for You


Puerto Rico sits in an interesting middle ground: it's a U.S. territory, so you don't need an international subsidiary to hire there, but it has its own tax code, labor laws, and compliance requirements that differ from any U.S. state. That distinction matters a lot when you're deciding how to structure your hiring.


Here's how the two main paths compare.


### Setting Up a Local Entity


Registering a Puerto Rico corporation or LLC gives you direct control over your workforce and can make sense if you're planning to hire 20 or more people on the island long-term. However, the setup process takes several weeks, requires legal and registered-agent fees, and obligates you to manage local payroll tax filings, Hacienda registration, and ongoing compliance independently. You'll also carry full employer liability from day one.


### Using an EOR


An Employer of Record in Puerto Rico takes on the legal employer role. Your team members work for you in practice, but the EOR handles payroll processing, local tax withholding, statutory benefits, and labor law compliance on your behalf. You can typically get someone working in days, not weeks, with no entity registration required.

## FAQs


### How does hiring through an employer of record in Puerto Rico differ from hiring in a U.S. state?


Puerto Rico follows both U.S. federal employment law and its own local labor code, which creates a wider compliance surface than any of the 50 states. Employers must account for Puerto Rico-specific requirements like Law 80 severance (meseta), mandatory Christmas bonus under Act 148, local income tax filings through Hacienda, and Workers' Compensation enrollment through the State Insurance Fund. None of these apply to mainland U.S. hires.


### Should I set up a local entity or use an employer of record in Puerto Rico?


An employer of record in Puerto Rico fits better when you're hiring one to five people, moving quickly, or testing the market without committing to permanent infrastructure. A local entity makes more sense if Puerto Rico becomes a core, long-term hiring market with 20 or more employees, where the fixed overhead of registration, legal fees, and ongoing compliance management becomes cost-effective relative to per-employee EOR fees.


### What payroll taxes apply to employees hired through an employer of record in Puerto Rico?


Employees in Puerto Rico are subject to both federal and territorial payroll obligations. FICA (Social Security and Medicare), federal income tax withholding, and FUTA apply just as they do for mainland U.S. workers. On top of that, employers must withhold Puerto Rico income tax under Act 1-2011, contribute to the local SUTA fund, and in some cases handle Chauffeurs' Social Security. An EOR manages all of these filings on your behalf.


### What's the fastest way to hire someone in Puerto Rico without opening a local entity?


Using an employer of record in Puerto Rico is the fastest path. With Bolto, onboarding typically completes within 48 hours of offer acceptance. Employment contracts, statutory benefit enrollment, payroll setup, and Department of Labor registration are all handled without you registering a local business entity first.
